This size corresponds to a wet weight of only 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], a mass that reflects the small diameter of the demersal, adhesive eggs from which they hatch, which typically measure around 0.8 mm. This initial body mass places the species among the smaller-bodied cobitids at the onset of the yolk-sac larval stage. During the initial days following chorion rupture, these lecithotrophic larvae rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves, a period that lasts until the mouth opens and active feeding commences. The progression from this minute hatchling to a fully grown adult involves a substantial increase in body size. Field surveys and laboratory growth studies have indicated that the maximum total length ultimately achieved by this species is 13.5 cm [Li = 13.5 cm], a milestone that defines the upper boundary of its somatic growth potential within its native European freshwater habitats.

The ultimate wet weight corresponding to the maximum body length is reported to be 12 grams [Wwi = 12 grams] in fully grown individuals, a value derived from length-weight regressions for the species. The developmental trajectory toward this adult size is punctuated by the onset of sexual maturity, which occurs at different sizes for males and females, a common pattern in teleost fishes. This size at female maturity is notably larger than that observed in males, reflecting the greater energetic demands of egg production. It also provides a useful metric for assessing population health; a reduction in this mean length at maturation can often signal the effects of size-selective fishing pressure or other environmental stressors on the population structure of this benthic species.

In contrast to the females, male Spined loaches attain sexual maturity at a considerably smaller body size, with the total length at puberty for males measured at 4 cm [Lp = 4 cm]. This earlier maturation in males is a common life-history strategy among iteroparous fishes, allowing them to begin contributing to the next generation before achieving their full somatic growth potential. This sex-specific divergence in mass at maturity underscores the differential allocation of resources between the sexes, with females directing a greater proportion of their energy intake toward the development of ovarian tissue and yolk-laden oocytes. Under controlled conditions maintained at 16 °C [T = 16 °C], a temperature typical of the species' preferred lotic habitats during the active growing season, the age at puberty for females has been estimated at 912 days [tp = 912 days], a substantial post-hatching developmental period.
